questions.question: You roll a fair six-sided die. Which statement about E[D] = 3.5 is correct?
options: It is the most likely single roll
It is a roll you will see about half the time
It is the long-run average, even though no roll ever equals 3.5
It only makes sense if you roll many dice at once
questions.explanation: Expectation is a probability-weighted average. It need not be a possible value: no face shows 3.5, but the average of many rolls approaches it.

questions.question: A network request succeeds independently with probability 0.2 on each try. What is the expected number of tries up to and including the first success?
questions.explanation: This is mean time to failure: E[F] = 1/p = 1/0.2 = 5. Using Pr[F > i] = 0.8^i and summing the geometric series gives the same result.

questions.question: You draw 5 cards from a shuffled 52-card deck. What is the expected number of aces?
options: It requires computing Pr[0], Pr[1], ..., Pr[4 aces] first
questions.explanation: Use one indicator per ace. Each specific ace is in your hand with probability 5/52, so E = 4 × 5/52 = 5/13. No binomial coefficients needed.

questions.question: Why can linearity of expectation be used to find the expected number of kids who get their own phone back, even though the events 'kid 1 matches' and 'kid 2 matches' are dependent?
options: Because the dependence is weak when n is large
Because linearity holds for any random variables on the same sample space, independent or not
Because the events are actually disjoint
Because we can multiply the probabilities instead
questions.explanation: Linearity needs no independence or disjointness. That is what makes it so powerful: sum the n indicators, each with expectation 1/n, to get exactly 1.
